source.title: The Geometry of Refusal: Linear Instability in Safety-Aligned LLMs

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests refusal steering with a different intervention: it contrasts output logits under safe and unrestricted system prompts and steers logits, rather than finding a residual-stream difference-in-means direction and ablating it across layers and positions.
record.gate_note: The study reports outcomes for its own contrastive-logit steering (CLS) interventions and its own hidden-state measurements. GCG results and the Arditi et al. activation-steering numbers are comparators or results from prior work, not results of the refusal-direction intervention being cataloged, so they are not recorded as rows. Text does not provide legible per-model values for the remaining points in Figure 3.
record.test_reason: The study does not test whether a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction mediates refusal. Its intervention, CLS, adds a per-token logit difference between an 'unrestricted' and a 'safe' system-prompt run of the same query. It pairs this with a forced 'Sure' prefix. The results are performance figures for this contrastive-decoding jailbreak and defense, compared against GCG and against Arditi et al.'s cited numbers. The one harmful-minus-benign mean-difference vector (Global Refusal Vector) is used only for cosine detection, which says nothing about causal mediation. PCA and KL-divergence analyses are correlational. So the study relies on the refusal-direction framing but does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also claim refusal is a linear feature along a single axis that is surface-level in Llama. They argue logit-level CLS exposes more fragility than activation steering (Arditi et al.), so the two approaches are complementary. They urge non-linear alignment that entangles safety with capability.
record.recipe_differences: The study contrasts logits from unrestricted and safe system prompts and adds a scaled logit-difference vector at decoding time; it also uses affirmative prefix injection for attacks. The original method derives a residual-stream difference-in-means direction and intervenes on residual activations, including projection/ablation across layers and positions. This paper's Global Refusal Vector is a final-layer hidden-state mean difference used for cosine detection, not the intervention used by CLS.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with steering coefficient alpha and model: Qwen-2.5 is reported as more resistant than Llama and Gemma. The paper reports different safe-versus-harmful divergence depths for Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5. Attack evaluation also uses prefix injection; the study focuses on single-turn interactions.

fits_no_version.finding: Contrastive logit steering (unrestricted minus safe system-prompt logits) plus a forced 'Sure' prefix jailbreaks models. Results: Gemma-3-12B 34% to 98% ASR at alpha 1; Llama >90% at alpha 2-3; Qwen-2.5-7B only 68.5% at alpha 5. JailbreakBench ASR 85-95% (Llama-3.1-8B) and 75-90% (Qwen-2.5-7B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-contrast logit steering with prefix injection bypasses refusal, with model-dependent resistance (Qwen more resistant).

fits_no_version.finding: Negative CLS lowers ASR: Llama-3.3-70B 68.8% to 9.4%; Gemma-3-12B to 6.0%. Qwen-2.5-7B coherence rises from 3.84 to 4.14 at alpha -2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inverting a prompt-contrast logit steer hardens models against jailbreaks at inference time.

fits_no_version.finding: A final-layer harmful-minus-benign mean vector detects malicious prompts by cosine similarity (F1 0.92 on Llama-3.1-8B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A mean-difference refusal vector serves as a zero-shot harmful-prompt detector.

fits_no_version.finding: Hidden-state KL divergence between safe and harmful trajectories appears only at the final layers in Llama-3.1 but at about 40% depth in Qwen-2.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safe-versus-harmful processing diverges at model-specific depths, which the authors link to steerability.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 6th Workshop on Trustworthy NLP (TrustNLP 2026), as stated
record.problems: No error bars, confidence intervals, or other uncertainty estimates are reported for the cataloged outcomes. Coherence is measured, but broad general capability is not. The authors note sensitivity to alpha, single-turn evaluation, and that their analysis does not disentangle architecture from training contributions. The primary judge was selected after comparison against 100 manually validated labels; the paper describes automated evaluation as noisy.
record.rows_left_out: No legible per-model values for the remaining Figure 3 alpha-sweep points are stated in the supplied text, so they are not separately extracted. GCG comparison outcomes and cited Arditi et al. results are excluded because they do not report the effect of the study's refusal-vector intervention.

untested.parts: No ablation of, or addition along, a harmful-minus-harmless residual direction. No measurement of refusal induced on harmless prompts via the direction. No capability preservation beyond a coherence score for the logit steer.
No analysis of whether existing jailbreaks suppress the direction. No adversarial training against ablation.
No comparison of single versus affine, cone or multi-direction accounts. The PCA 'single axis' claim rests on a 2D plot with PC1 at 28%.
Harm judgment and refusal decision are not separated.
No transfer across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct.
Training is mentioned only as speculation; the authors say causal attribution remains future work.

missing.what: Positive-steering results for Llama-3.3-70B and Gemma-3 described as a 'binary' failure mode; no values given except Gemma-3-12B. Rows for Gemma-3-4B and Qwen-2.5-1.5B exist only in the Figure 3 heatmap.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the CLS rows to V1 and V3, but CLS is contrastive decoding between system-prompt personas plus a forced prefix. It is not the difference-in-means direction V1 names, and not a test of how other jailbreaks work (V3). Table 2's Arditi figures are cited, not rerun, and evaluation protocols may differ. Row r6 misassigns a positive-steering value to a negative-steering condition. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The judge is Mistral-Small, validated on 100 labels.

versions.untested_parts: CLS is a logit-space intervention, not residual-stream projection or ablation at every layer and position. The study does not test whether adding the direction makes the model refuse harmless requests, and does not comprehensively test preservation of general capabilities.
No weight edit or abliteration of released model weights is tested.

The study tests its own CLS attack, which deliberately steers against safety, not whether other jailbreaks naturally work by suppressing this direction. It does not train models against the ablation or test robustness from such training.
No comparison of affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts is reported.
The study does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Models are steered using their own prompt-derived vectors; transfer of a direction across languages, model variants, or from base to instruct models is not tested.
The study speculates that architecture and training shape refusal topology but does not compare training procedures or stages or establish a training-dependent cause.
No reasoning models or reasoning-before-answer behavior are tested.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Constructed a final-layer Global Refusal Vector by subtracting mean benign-query activations from mean harmful-query activations, then classified prompts by cosine similarity.
rows.measure: Malicious-versus-benign classification F1 using cosine similarity to the vector
rows.value: F1 = 0.92; benign queries typically around 0.16 cosine similarity and malicious queries around 0.65
rows.note: This supports linear detectability but does not establish that the vector causally mediates refusal.
rows.check: A harmful-minus-benign final-layer mean difference used for detection (F1 0.92). Detection does not test V1's causal mediation. Threshold is not stated.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Positive CLS on Gemma-3-12B and Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.2-3B under the reported harmful-request evaluations
reader_labels.reason: Positive steering yields 98% ASR for Gemma-3-12B and greater than 90% for the reported Llama series, consistent with a strong refusal-bypassing effect in these settings (r1, r4, r5, r11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Qwen-2.5-7B positive CLS and high-magnitude alpha-sweep setting
reader_labels.reason: ASR remains 68.5% at alpha 5.0 in the sweep and is 75% and 90% at alpha 2 and 3 on JailbreakBench; high steering also substantially lowers Gemma-3-12B coherence (r2, r3, r12, r13).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The paper's own CLS attack with prefix injection on JailbreakBench and HarmBench harmful-request prompts
reader_labels.reason: The deliberately applied CLS attack attains 75–95% ASR on JailbreakBench and 73% and 91% on the two reported HarmBench models (r10, r11, r12, r13, r14, r15).
